newsitem.title: USA: US defensive stocks seen benefiting from rate hike.
newsitem.headline: US defensive stocks seen benefiting from rate hike.

text.p: Defensive stocks such as food, tobacco and other consumer non-durables will benefit from the Federal Reserve's decision to raise short-term interest rates, analysts said.
The losers will be manufacturers of big-ticket items -- homebuilders, auto-makers and appliance manufacturers -- which depend on ready consumer credit, they said.

Drug stocks rallied Tuesday and held their gains after the Fed announced a quarter-point rise in the federal funds rate. Merck & Co Inc was up 1-1/2 at 91-3/8 and Warner-Lambert Co added 2-5/8 to 92-1/8.
Shares of tobacco giant Philip Morris Cos Inc were up two at 117-7/8.

"The (rate) hike should give a boost to defensive areas such as the utility companies, healthcare, tobacco and personal care companies like Gillette and Avon Products," said Anthony O'Bryan, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.

"People tend to cut back on these items last. They will postpone buying a new home or a car and will make do with what they have. But they will keep on buying groceries and cigarettes; they will keep paying their utility bills," he said.
Not all analysts are positive about defensive issues. Some say the stocks have already had a strong run in anticipation of the rate hike and that any new rally may be short-lived.
"Theoretically, a rate hike should not have great effect on consumer non-durables," said Ricky Harrington, technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane.

"Tobaccos, food and drugs have moved up over a long period of time in this bull market, so they won't perform their historic function of being defensive because they are overvalued," the analyst said.
Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp, said each bit of inflation and employment data will be scrutinized for clues about when and by how much the Fed will move again.
"Wall Street believes that one rate increase is usually followed by more. It's not only a historical pattern, but the Fed rarely gets ahead of the inflation curve," Johnson said.
Wall Street will now debate whether Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has done too little too late, or if he has beaten price pressures to the punch, he said.
"Some believe that we are already seeing upward pressure on prices and that it is too late," Johnson said. "Others, like me, believe that it is not too late.
"That is the debate that will rage on Wall Street."
